Likely causes

Common Dryer Problems: A Look at Our Repairs

Dryer Not Heating

We check the heating parts, controls and airflow before recommending any part.

Not Heating: Damaged Igniter and Overheating

We found a damaged igniter, a faulty high-limit thermostat, and lint restricting airflow.

See this repairHide details

When we opened this gas dryer, we found heavy lint buildup around the burner. The igniter had partly broken apart, but that wasn’t the only thing that needed attention.

By the time we took the burner-area photo, we had already vacuumed away much of the lint around the burner. You can still see what remained.

Lint was restricting airflow, and we also found that the high-limit thermostat wasn’t cutting off the heat properly. That thermostat is there to help protect the dryer from overheating.

Simply fitting a new igniter would have left those other problems in place. We replaced the igniter, high-limit thermostat, thermal fuse, and temperature sensor, and cleaned the affected areas inside the dryer.

We also checked the drum rollers. They had buildup around them, but we found no damage that called for replacement. We cleaned them as part of the service rather than add unnecessary parts to the repair bill. After servicing, the drum ran without the extra squeaking or rattling.

Some stubborn dark staining remained on the metal. We removed the lint and debris, but didn’t try to polish every hidden surface back to a shine. The goal was to address the buildup and repair the faults we found, rather than make the inside look brand new.

This is why we look beyond the first damaged part. A dryer not heating can involve more than the part that produces or starts the heat.

Our advice? Clean the lint screen after every load. If clothes start taking longer to dry, don’t just keep adding another cycle. And if you notice a burning smell, stop using the dryer and have it checked.

Dryer Not Drying Clothes

A dryer can turn and heat but still leave clothes damp when airflow is lost.

Not Drying: Lint Blocking the Internal Airflow

The components were working. Clearing the lint blockage and servicing the dryer was all it needed.

See this repairHide details

Here’s another situation we see: a dryer isn’t drying clothes properly, but nothing actually needs replacing. The problem is lint blocking the airflow.

That’s what we found here. We checked the components, and they were working. So we gave the dryer a thorough service: cleaned the rollers, cleared the blockages, vacuumed the inside, and ran it afterward to check its operation.

No replacement parts were needed. This time, maintenance was enough.

A small tip from us: clean the lint screen after every load. If drying starts taking longer even with a clean screen, there may be a blockage farther along the airflow path.

Not Drying: Clogged Dryer Vent

The dryer was heating, but lint in the exhaust duct was restricting airflow.

See this repairHide details

Sometimes the dryer is working, but the clothes still aren’t drying properly. That was the situation here: nothing in the dryer needed replacing, but lint had built up in the exhaust path.

We found buildup in the connecting duct and at the wall connection. The dryer could produce heat, but the restricted airflow was stopping it from carrying the moist air away properly.

No appliance parts needed replacing. What was needed was dryer vent cleaning to clear the blockage, rather than a repair inside the dryer.

How quickly a dryer vent collects lint varies from home to home. On service visits, we’ve seen heavily blocked vents after around five years, and others that were still relatively clear after much longer. That doesn’t mean it’s a good idea to wait until drying stops.

The length of the exhaust duct, the number of bends, how often the dryer is used, and the installation all make a difference. A long run to a roof outlet can create more resistance to airflow than a short, direct route outside.

A small tip: cleaning the lint screen doesn’t replace dryer vent cleaning. The general recommendation is to clean the exhaust duct once a year, or sooner if drying starts taking longer.

We inspect dryer vent restrictions and clean dryer vents that exit through an exterior side wall. We do not clean vents that exit through the roof. We’ll explain what we find and the work needed before proceeding.

Heating but Not Drying: Cracked Blower Wheel

The drum turned and the dryer heated, but a cracked blower wheel wasn’t moving enough air.

See this repairHide details

We started with a quick airflow check. A paper towel held at the intake wasn’t being pulled against it as we would expect. Something wasn’t moving air properly. The question was why.

We checked for lint blockages and looked at the drive components. Finding the answer took more disassembly than expected on this GE stacked washer-dryer.

The blower wheel was still turning, which made the fault easy to miss. But it wasn’t turning consistently with the motor. Once we removed it, we found that it had cracked.

That explained why the dryer could seem to be working while still leaving clothes damp. This wasn’t a blockage that cleaning would solve. The blower wheel needed replacing.

The drum was turning, the heat was there, but the cracked blower wheel wasn’t moving enough air. That was the missing piece.

Dryer Making Noise

We check for buildup and wear before deciding what needs replacing.

Squeaking Noise: Buildup Around the Drum Rollers

Hair and lint were restricting the rollers. Cleaning and servicing resolved the noise without new rollers.

See this repairHide details

This dryer was making noise, but the drum rollers themselves were still in good condition. Hair and lint had collected around them, making it harder for them to turn freely.

Once we opened it up, we could check the rollers and their shafts rather than assume they all needed replacing.

We removed the buildup, cleaned the rollers and their shafts, and checked them for wear. There was no damage that called for replacement, so we serviced the existing parts and tested the dryer afterward.

The noise was gone. No new rollers were needed.

That isn’t always how it goes. If a roller has stopped turning and developed a flat spot, or its shaft has worn a groove, cleaning won’t undo that damage. Those parts need replacing.

A small tip from us: don’t wait for a squeak to become a loud grinding or thumping noise. Having it checked early may mean the existing parts can still be serviced, as they could here.

Dryer Not Spinning

A stopped drum does not always mean a failed motor.

Not Spinning: A Blocked Blower

Lint had jammed the blower. Clearing the blockages resolved the problem without replacing the motors.

See this repairHide details

In these two repairs, lint buildup had jammed the blower. The dryers had stopped turning, but neither needed a new motor.

In the first dryer, we found a torn lint screen that had been letting lint through. Over time, the buildup interfered with the blower’s rotation. On this design, the same motor drives the blower and the drum belt, so a jammed blower can stop the drum too.

A torn lint screen also needs attention so it does not keep allowing lint into the dryer. Clearing the blockage alone does not resolve that issue.

We found a similar blockage in another dryer:

Both owners stopped using their dryers and called when they noticed the drum wasn’t turning. We cleared the blockages and cleaned the affected areas. The motors were still working, so no motor replacement was needed.

Sometimes a dryer in this condition can still turn while empty, then struggle or stop once wet clothes are added. That doesn’t necessarily mean the load is too large. Something may be making the motor work harder than it should.

Our advice? If the drum stops turning, don’t keep restarting the dryer, try to help it along by hand, or work around the problem with smaller loads. Have it checked. Catching a blockage before it causes further damage may keep a straightforward cleaning from becoming a more expensive repair.

FAQ

Dryer repair FAQs

My dryer runs but won't heat. Can you fix it?

Almost always yes, and usually in one visit. On an electric dryer it is the heating element or a thermal fuse; on a gas dryer it is the igniter. Our vans carry all three.

How much will it cost?

It depends which part failed. The service visit is free when you approve the repair and $80 if you decide not to go ahead, and you get the full price before any work starts.

It takes three cycles to dry one load.

That is nearly always airflow rather than heat. The heat is being made but it is not being moved through the clothes, either because the blower wheel is worn or because the venting behind the machine is restricted. We measure the airflow and tell you which it is.

Is a long drying time actually a problem?

Yes, and not only for your power bill. Restricted airflow makes the dryer overheat, which trips the high-limit thermostat and, over time, kills the heating element. It is also the condition behind most dryer fires.

Do you clean dryer vents?

Yes. We clean dryer vents that exit through an exterior side wall. We do not clean vents that exit through the roof. Tell us where the vent exits when you request service.

My dryer squeals when it turns.

Usually the drum rollers, the idler pulley or the belt. We check each one and replace what is actually worn; a part that is still in good shape can be cleaned and left in place.

My dryer stops part-way through a cycle.

It can be overheating and tripping the high-limit thermostat, often because airflow is restricted. It can also be the motor or the controls. We find what is causing it before replacing the thermostat, or it can simply trip again.

The drum isn't turning at all.

Usually a snapped belt, which is an inexpensive fix. Sometimes the drive motor. We check the belt first rather than quoting the motor straight away.

Do you repair stacked and closet-installed units?

Yes. They have to be pulled and partly dismantled to be reached, which is why some companies avoid them. It is routine work for us.

How long does a dryer repair take?

Most are done in a single visit, usually around an hour. We usually carry common elements, igniters, fuses and belts; a model-specific part may need ordering.

What warranty do I get?

Our labor carries 90 days on every completed repair, and original manufacturer (OEM) parts carry a full year. We tell you which parts are going in before you approve the work.

Still not sure?

Call and describe it. We will tell you straight whether it is worth fixing.
